clinicalPearls: Combination of diffuse transgredient palmoplantar keratoderma with severe, early-onset (aggressive) periodontitis
Periodontal destruction affects both primary and permanent dentitions, often causing premature loss of teeth in childhood
The keratoderma may extend onto the dorsa of the hands and feet, elbows and knees, and can be associated with hyperhidrosis and malodour
Autosomal recessive; caused by loss-of-function mutations in CTSC encoding cathepsin C (dipeptidyl peptidase I)
Increased susceptibility to pyogenic skin and systemic infections, including a recognised risk of liver abscess
Consanguinity is often present in affected families
Management combines emollients/keratolytics and oral retinoids for the skin with intensive periodontal care/dental preservation for Papillon-Lefevre
reference.pathophysiology: Papillon-Lefevre syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in CTSC, which encodes cathepsin C (dipeptidyl peptidase I). Cathepsin C activates a range of serine proteases stored in immune and inflammatory cells, including neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G and granzymes. Its deficiency impairs neutrophil and immune-cell function, reducing the ability to control bacteria at the gingival margin and skin, which produces aggressive periodontitis and heightened susceptibility to pyogenic infection. In the epidermis, disturbed protease-mediated regulation of keratinocyte differentiation contributes to the diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma. The combined immune and epidermal effects explain the characteristic skin-and-gum phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Haim-Munk syndrome (allelic CTSC disorder with additional features)
Other diffuse hereditary palmoplantar keratodermas without periodontitis
Leucocyte adhesion deficiency and other neutrophil disorders
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of CTSC and assay of cathepsin C activity
Dental and periodontal assessment with orthopantomogram/radiographs of alveolar bone
Skin biopsy of keratoderma (hyperkeratosis with variable inflammation)
Microbiological evaluation and imaging if pyogenic or hepatic infection is suspected
Screening for consanguinity and family history
redFlags: Rapid periodontal breakdown with mobility or loss of teeth
Fever with right-upper-quadrant pain suggesting liver abscess
Recurrent or deep pyogenic skin infection
Systemic sepsis in a susceptible individual
reference.prognosis: The keratoderma is chronic but manageable; the major morbidity is early loss of the dentition, which intensive periodontal care and dental preservation can mitigate. With attention to infection risk, general prognosis is good, although recurrent pyogenic infection and periodontal disease persist.
pitfalls: Treating the keratoderma without engaging dental services, leading to preventable tooth loss
Overlooking the increased infection risk, including occult liver abscess
Confusing it with common palmoplantar keratoderma and missing the periodontal association
Delaying genetic diagnosis in consanguineous families where recurrence risk is high
management: Oral retinoids such as acitretin, which improve the palmoplantar keratoderma and can help preserve the dentition when started early
Intensive periodontal therapy with regular mechanical debridement, chlorhexidine mouthwash and courses of systemic antibiotics such as amoxicillin with metronidazole around tooth eruption
Topical keratolytics and emollients for the palmoplantar keratoderma, with attention to hyperhidrosis and secondary infection
Dental rehabilitation including extraction of hopeless teeth and prosthetic or implant-based restoration to maintain function
Prompt treatment of pyogenic skin and systemic infections with vigilance for liver abscess
Genetic counselling and CTSC testing for the family, with screening of at-risk relatives given autosomal recessive inheritance and frequent consanguinity
Coordinated dermatology, periodontology and clinical genetics care
